1	# Join keys and the normalization ladder
2	
3	Load this before joining anything.
4	
5	## Why this file exists
6	
7	A plant does not have one database. It has five to eight systems bought at
8	different times by different departments, and the same physical thing carries a
9	different identifier in each one. A single part might be:
10	
11	| Where | How it appears |
12	|---|---|
13	| ERP item master | `PN-4471-B` |
14	| MES production export | `4471B` |
15	| Quality inspection export | `4471-B Rev 2` |
16	| Maintenance spares list | `Bracket, Upper, 4471` |
17	
18	All four are the same part. Only the first three are joinable, and none of them
19	match as-is.
20	
21	## The six join keys
22	
23	These are the identifiers that should be common across systems. Everything the
24	consolidated dataset is built around hangs off one of them.
25	
26	| Join key | Links | Source of truth |
27	|---|---|---|
28	| Part number | Product ↔ production ↔ quality ↔ purchasing | ERP item master (NetSuite or Infor M3) |
29	| Production work order number | Production run ↔ output ↔ quality results ↔ cost | The ERP. In Infor M3 it is the manufacturing order number |
30	| Sales order number | Customer commitment ↔ production ↔ shipping | The ERP. In Infor M3 it is the customer order number |
31	| Lot / batch number | Material ↔ parts made from it ↔ customers who received them | MES or quality export |
32	| Asset ID | Machine ↔ downtime ↔ maintenance history | CMMS connector or maintenance export |
33	| Supplier ID / vendor number | Purchase orders ↔ incoming material ↔ supplier quality | The ERP |
34	
35	**Source of truth decides direction.** When two sides disagree on a key's shape,
36	normalize toward the source of truth rather than toward whichever side has more
37	rows. The ERP item master is the reference for part numbers even when the MES
38	export has ten times the volume.
39	
40	### The work order name collision
41	
42	Maintenance systems also call their repair tickets "work orders." A production
43	work order and a maintenance work order are different records with different
44	numbering, and joining one to the other produces nonsense.
45	
46	Always disambiguate in output and in column naming: **production work order** and
47	**maintenance work order**, never bare "work order" or "WO."
48	
49	## The normalization ladder
50	
51	Apply in this order. Each rung is more aggressive than the last, so stopping
52	early is safer than going further than needed.
53	
54	| Rung | Transformation | Notes |
55	|---|---|---|
56	| 1 | Trim leading and trailing whitespace | Manual exports carry trailing spaces constantly |
57	| 2 | Normalize case | Fold to a single case for comparison only |
58	| 3 | Normalize punctuation | `PN-4471-B` / `PN_4471_B` / `PN4471B` collapse to one comparison form. A lost part prefix (`4471B` against `PN-4471-B`) collapses too, **only where exactly one part on the `parts` tab matches once its prefix is dropped**. Name the prefix in the log. Where two or more parts would match (`PN-4471-B` and `AX-4471-B`), nothing is matched by this rung: the record is reported with every candidate, and the plant says which |
59	| 4 | Restore lost leading zeros | `451` matches `00451` only if a zero-padded variant exists on the other side. Test for it; do not pad blindly |
60	| 5 | Strip revision suffix | `4471-B` matches `4471-B Rev 2`. The revision is extra information, not a different part |
61	
62	**Rungs 1, 2 and 3 are safe to propose as automatic.** Rungs 4 and 5 change
63	meaning and always carry their own proposal, because a stripped revision or an
64	assumed zero can be wrong.
65	
66	### Two hard rules
67	
68	**Compare on the normalized form; store and display the original.** The
69	consolidated dataset carries the source system's own identifier verbatim
70	alongside the normalized key. A plant person searching for `PN-4471-B` in their
71	own vocabulary must find it. Never overwrite a source identifier with a
72	normalized one.
73	
74	**Every normalization applied is logged and reportable.** The data quality report
75	names each rule that fired, how many records it touched, and an example of the
76	before and after. A silent normalization is indistinguishable from a bug, and the
77	first time a total looks wrong this log is the only way to tell them apart.
78	
79	### Revision data is preserved, never discarded
80	
81	When rung 5 fires, the revision that was stripped goes into its own column and
82	the report states that revision data existed on one side only. Stripping it to
83	make the join work is correct; losing it is not.
84	
85	## Date windows by entity
86	
87	When the user narrows the join to the overlap, the window does not apply to
88	every tab alike. Three kinds of record, three rules:
89	
90	| Kind | Tabs | What the window does |
91	|---|---|---|
92	| **Activity** | `production_output`, `downtime_events`, `inspection_results`, `plan`, `operation_actuals` | Scoped to the overlap. A row outside it is Class 7 |
93	| **Open commitments** | Open `sales_orders` lines, open `production_work_orders` | **Kept by status, whatever their dates.** An open order is in scope until it closes. A sales order line that carries only a promised date and no order date is never out of window for lacking one |
94	| **Reference history** | `purchase_orders` and their receipts, `maintenance_work_orders`, `ncrs`, `lots` | Kept for a lookback before the window start: the Plant context's lookback if one is set, otherwise **180 days, stated as a default, not plant-set**. Labelled as history in the report and never counted in the window's totals |
95	
96	Closed commitments (a shipped sales order, a closed work order) are activity:
97	scoped by their own close or ship date. Never class a record 7 because the
98	narrowing removed the history that explains it. A material receipt from
99	before the window is how a heat is traced to the work orders it fed, and a
100	repair from June is how a breakdown is read in August.
101	
102	...[truncated]

1	# The eight mismatch classes
2	
3	Load this when classifying join failures.
4	
5	When two datasets are joined on a key, some rows find no partner. That is not a
6	nuisance to be counted — it is usually a real business problem in disguise. The
7	skill classifies every mismatch into one of the eight classes below and reports
8	each class separately, with counts **and example rows**.
9	
10	**A count on its own is not a finding.** "312 mismatches" tells a plant person
11	nothing they can act on. "298 of them are one export covering three days the
12	other does not" tells them to re-run tomorrow.
13	
14	---
15	
16	## Check the date window first
17	
18	**Class 7 is checked before any other class is reported.** A date-window
19	mismatch manufactures apparent mismatches across every key at once, and it
20	explains most large mismatch counts. Reporting format drift and orphan records
21	on top of an unnoticed window gap sends someone chasing problems that do not
22	exist.
23	
24	Order of work: window overlap, then key shape, then genuine one-sided records.
25	
26	---
27	
28	## Class 1 — Orphan record
29	
30	**What it is.** A record references a key that does not exist on the other side
31	at all. A production record reports output against production work order
32	`WO-88213`, and no such work order exists in NetSuite.
33	
34	**What it means.** One of three things, and they are very different: somebody ran
35	an unauthorized job, a work order was deleted after the fact, or the two exports
36	are from different dates.
37	
38	**Detection.** Key is well-formed and no normalization rung produces a match.
39	
40	**Proposed fix.** None automatic — this is a question, not a formatting problem.
41	Report the orphans with their quantities and dates, and state which of the three
42	explanations the surrounding evidence supports. Check the date window before
43	concluding anything.
44	
45	**On routings: routing with no matching part.** A routing whose part number no
46	normalization rung matches to the item master. Either the part was renamed,
47	retired, or never set up in the item master. Report it by that name, with its
48	operations; no automatic fix. It is never used to quote a part it merely looks
49	like.
50	
51	---
52	
53	## Class 2 — Format drift
54	
55	**What it is.** `PN-4471-B` versus `4471B` versus `4471_B`. Same part, different
56	punctuation.
57	
58	**What it means.** Nothing about the business. It is the most common class by
59	volume and the least interesting.
60	
61	**Detection.** Normalization ladder rungs 1–3 produce a match.
62	
63	**Proposed fix.** Apply the punctuation and case normalization, with the
64	normalization shown.
65	
66	---
67	
68	## Class 3 — Leading-zero loss
69	
70	**What it is.** `00451` became `451` because a system exported to CSV and a
71	spreadsheet stripped the zeros on open.
72	
73	**What it means.** A tooling artifact, extremely common, and not a data entry
74	problem.
75	
76	**Detection.** Rung 4 — test whether a zero-padded variant of the short key
77	exists on the other side. Do not pad blindly; only claim the class when the
78	padded partner is actually present.
79	
80	**Proposed fix.** Restore the padding to the source-of-truth width. Report the
81	width used.
82	
83	---
84	
85	## Class 4 — Revision suffix mismatch
86	
87	**What it is.** `4471-B` versus `4471-B Rev 2`. The part is the same; the
88	revision is additional information carried on one side only.
89	
90	**What it means.** One system tracks revision on the identifier and the other
91	does not.
92	
93	**Detection.** Rung 5 — a match appears once the revision suffix is stripped.
94	
95	**Proposed fix.** Strip and match, preserve the stripped revision in its own
96	column, and report that revision data existed on one side only. Never discard it.
97	
98	**On routings: routing revision mismatch — no automatic fix.** A routing
99	written for revision 1, read against a drawing at revision 2, matches once the
100	suffix is stripped, and that match is exactly the mistake. A routing is the
101	operation list for one revision; a later revision may have tightened a
102	tolerance that adds an operation. Report it as a *routing revision mismatch*:
103	which revision the routing is for, which revision is being quoted or is
104	current, and what the drawing's revision history says changed where it is
105	available. The routing stays on the `routings` tab, marked `revision_mismatch`,
106	and `quote-build` shows it as superseded, never prices from it. A routing with
107	no revision at all is not a mismatch but it is not a match either: report it
108	as revision-unknown, never assumed current. `quote-build` may use it only with
109	that label on every line it touches.
110	
111	---
112	
113	## Class 5 — Case and whitespace
114	
115	**What it is.** Trailing spaces and inconsistent capitalization, usually from a
116	manual export or a hand-maintained sheet.
117	
118	**Detection.** Rungs 1–2 produce a match.
119	
120	**Proposed fix.** Trim and case-fold for comparison.
121	
122	---
123	
124	## Class 6 — Genuine one-sided record
125	
126	**What it is.** A part in the ERP that has never been produced. A machine in
127	the CMMS that appears in no production record. A supplier with no purchase orders
128	in the window.
129	
130	**What it means.** Usually nothing wrong at all. An item master legitimately
131	contains parts that are not currently running.
132	
133	**Detection.** Key is well-formed, no normalization produces a match, and the
134	absence is consistent with the record's own type and dates.
135	
136	**Proposed fix.** None. **Report, do not alarm.** Distinguish this class clearly
137	from Class 1, because an orphan is a problem and a one-sided record generally is
138	not, and conflating them makes the whole report look like noise.
139	
140	**Unless another source contradicts it.** A closed production work order with
141	no MES output is one-sided; the same work order cited on an NCR, on inspection

1	# Contract: the consolidated dataset
2	
3	**Emitted by** `data-consolidate`
4	**Consumed by** every data-dependent skill — as the default source, not the
5	only one; see *What this dataset is authoritative for* below — and it is the
6	mapping target for `custom-connector`
7	**Chain** 1, RFQ to quote (step 2) and 3, Morning plant pulse (step 1)
8	**Contract version** 6
9	
10	Rules that govern every contract are in [README.md](README.md).
11	
12	This file names the tabs
13	and columns so a consumer and a producer cannot invent two different shapes.
14	
15	---
16	
17	## Form
18	
19	One queryable working file. **Excel workbook, one tab per entity, is the v1
20	format. The writer is swappable.** The shape below is the contract.
21	
22	If `data-consolidate` pulled a record type, that type has a tab. A pulled input
23	with no tab is how inventory went missing the first time this file was written.
24	
25	---
26	
27	## Entity tabs
28	
29	The join hangs off five anchors: part, production work order,
30	sales order, lot, asset. Every other input is an entity too. It gets its
31	own tab. It is not folded onto an anchor.
32	
33	### The five anchors
34	
35	| Tab | Grain | Key | Fields |
36	|---|---|---|---|
37	| `parts` | One row per part | Part number | Description, standard cost, UOM |
38	| `production_work_orders` | One row per production work order | Production work order number | Part, qty ordered, due date, status, and from version 5 the sales order it is built for (`sales_order` / `sales_order_verbatim`, null where the source holds no link). From version 6, closed-job cost where the ERP holds it: `actual_material_cost`, `actual_labor_cost`, `actual_burden_cost`, `actual_subcontract_cost` (each with `currency`), `qty_completed`, `closed_date`, `revision`, all nullable |
39	| `sales_orders` | One row per sales order line | Sales order number | Customer, part, qty, promised date, price |
40	| `lots` | One row per lot or batch | Lot number | The identity stamped on a quantity of material |
41	| `assets` | One row per machine | Asset ID | Location |
42	
43	### The other inputs
44	
45	| Tab | Grain | Joins on | Fields |
46	|---|---|---|---|
47	| `inventory` | One row per part per location | Part | On-hand qty, location |
48	| `purchase_orders` | One row per PO line | Part, supplier ID | Supplier, part, qty, cost, delivery date |
49	| `production_output` | One row per work order per shift per production day | Production work order, part | Qty good, qty scrap, shift, production day. **Two rows at the same grain are a duplicate key (class 8); the same work order on another shift is not** |
50	| `downtime_events` | One row per stoppage | Asset | Start, end, reason code |
51	| `inspection_results` | One row per measurement | Lot or production work order | Measurement vs spec |
52	| `maintenance_work_orders` | One row per maintenance ticket | Asset | Maintenance work order, dates, close-out notes |
53	| `plan` | One row per part per date | Part | Planned qty, date |
54	| `ncrs` | One row per NCR | Production work order, part, lot | NCR ID, found at, description verbatim, status, customer. |
55	
56	`inventory` is on-hand **by part and location**. A single on-hand total on
57	`parts` is not this tab. Containment needs the location.
58	
59	Supplier is a join key, not an anchor. It lives on `purchase_orders`.
60	
61	**`ncrs` is where an NCR export lands, and the NCR-to-work-order check runs on
62	it**: the NCR's part against the part the ERP holds for the work order it
63	cites, and its date against that work order's first recorded output.
64	`ncr-writeup` and `root-cause-capa` still read the NCR export raw for the
65	record as written; they read this tab for whether its part label can be
66	trusted.
67	
68	### Routings and operation actuals
69	
70	Two more inputs, for quoting. They are what `quote-build` derives
71	machine hours from before it ever opens a model, and the order matters: a
72	current-revision routing or a trustworthy set of actuals makes the design step
73	a cross-check rather than the basis.
74	
75	| Tab | Grain | Joins on | Fields |
76	|---|---|---|---|
77	| `routings` | One row per part, revision and operation | Part | `part_revision`, `op_seq`, `work_center` / `work_center_verbatim`, `cell`, `setup_hours`, `run_time_per_unit`, `run_time_unit`, `time_unit_flag`, `routing_mismatch` |
78	| `operation_actuals` | One row per production work order and operation | Production work order, part | `op_seq`, `work_center` / `work_center_verbatim`, `cell`, `actual_setup_hours`, `actual_run_hours`, `qty_completed`, `uom`, `closed_date`, `time_unit_flag`, `actuals_confidence`, `confidence_reason` |
79	
80	Column behavior on both tabs:
81	
82	| Column | Type | Behavior | Notes |
83	|---|---|---|---|
84	| `part_revision` | string or null | Degrades on `routings` | The revision the routing was written for. **Null is not "current"**: a routing with no revision is reported as revision-unknown, never assumed to match the drawing |
85	| `op_seq` | integer | Required | As the source numbers it |
86	| `work_center` / `work_center_verbatim` | string | Required | A pair, like a join key, though it is not one of the six |

88	| `setup_hours`, `run_time_per_unit` | number | Required | As the source states them. **Never converted** |
89	| `run_time_unit` | enum | Required | `min`, `h`, or `undeclared`. Read from the header or a unit column, never inferred from the size of the number |
90	| `time_unit_flag` | string or null | Degrades | Set when a unit is undeclared, or when this tab's unit differs from the other tab's for the same part and operation. Names both units. No conversion is computed |

1	# Computed figures — a number is printed, never retyped
2	
3	**Shared across the plugin.** Every skill that reports a number follows this.
4	
5	The failure this exists to stop has one shape. The skill does the work
6	correctly, then writes the summary from memory. The summary says "eleven
7	maintenance records" where the data holds six, "3.1× the control limit" where
8	the division gives 2.36, "five orders" where the file has six — the customer's
9	own order being the one missed. Each figure is stated with total confidence,
10	and each is the first thing a quality manager or an estimator will check.
11	
12	A second shape sits next to it: the confident absence. "The sister machine has
13	no bearing history." "There is no PM plan in the library." Said after one
14	search, about a record that was there.
15	
16	---
17	
18	## The rule
19	
20	**Every count, total, ratio, percentage and "N of M" in user-facing output is
21	produced by code run over the data in this session, and printed from that
22	result. A number is never retyped, rounded from memory, or paraphrased.**
23	
24	**A negative claim — "has no history," "no plan exists," "not in the file" —
25	cites the exact query or filter that returned nothing.** Where the search tool
26	may be incomplete (SharePoint search under-reports), enumerate the folder
27	instead, or say *"not found by search"* rather than *"does not exist."* Those
28	are different claims and only the first one was earned.
29	
30	---
31	
32	## The figures block — a required part of the output
33	
34	A rule that says "check your numbers" is a rule nobody can see being skipped.
35	So the check is an output, not an intention.
36	
37	**Every run that reports a number emits a figures block**, produced by code,
38	before the prose that uses it. One row per figure:
39	
40	| Figure | Value | Computed from | Filter or query |
41	|---|---|---|---|
42	| Maintenance records, HAAS-VF4-02 | 9 | maintenance export | `asset_id == "HAAS-VF4-02"` |
43	| Sibling records mentioning "bearing" | 2 (LMB-13781, LMB-14022, both HAAS-VF4-05) | maintenance export | same model, `notes` contains "bearing" |
44	| Measured ÷ upper control limit | 1.87 | inspection export | measured and limit both from the same computation |
45	| PM plan documents found | 0 — **not found by search** | M365 library | search "PM plan"; folder not enumerated |
46	
47	Then three things hold, and a reader can check all three without re-running
48	anything:
49	
50	1. **The prose quotes the block.** A number that appears in the narrative, a
51	   table or a headline appears in the block with the same value. A number in
52	   the prose with no row in the block is a defect.
53	2. **A ratio comes from the same computation as its parts.** Do not compute a
54	   control limit in code and then divide by it in your head.
55	3. **A subtotal reconciles to its total in the block itself.** If 126 records
56	   matched, the exact and normalized rows add to 126, and each equals the sum
57	   of the classes it is made of. A block that does not add up is fixed before
58	   anything is written from it.
59	
60	Where the skill already emits "the structured data behind the report," the
61	figures block is part of it. Where the output is a controlled document going to
62	a customer or supplier, the block stays on the internal side.
63	
64	---
65	
66	## When no code can be run
67	
68	Some sessions have no code execution. Then the count was made by reading, and
69	the output says so: **"counted by reading, not computed — verify before
70	relying on it,"** on the block and beside any figure that matters. Never
71	present a hand count as a computed one. This is `absent-is-not-zero.md` applied
72	to the method rather than the data: an unverified number named as unverified is
73	useful, and one dressed as computed is worse than none.
74	
75	---
76	
77	## What this does not change
78	
79	- A figure that cannot be read is still reported unreadable. The block carries
80	  the row with the reason, never a guess.
81	- Rates, whether read from an `MFG_*` variable or the plant profile, follow
82	  `secret-config.md`. The block names the source; the value appears only where
83	  the audience rule allows.
84	- Computing a figure is not applying a fix. Anything that changes data still
85	  needs its yes.

I've joined the six files into one dataset and written the data quality report. Part numbers and production work orders all match, but **none of the machine IDs match the equipment list**.

I couldn't run code in this session, so every count below was made by reading the files. The files are tiny (17 data rows), but verify the counts before relying on them. For the same reason the dataset is one CSV per tab, not an Excel workbook.

---

**DECISION REQUIRED: APPROVE OR REJECT**
**Cell label `CELL-A` (production output file) = `Cell A` (equipment list).**
- **Why:** the two labels are identical once case and punctuation are ignored.
- **Limits:** cell is a label, not a key. Approving this links no machines.
- **Rows touched:** 3 output rows (WO-1001, WO-1002, WO-1003: 1,000 good and 15 scrap, unit not stated) and 2 equipment rows (HMC-01, VMC-02).
- **Approve:** both labels count as one cell when rolling up by cell. The original spellings are kept.
- **Reject:** the labels stay separate and I won't propose this again.
- **Reply:** "approve cell CELL-A = Cell A" or "reject", with the name of the person approving.

---

**Freshness: the drop only covers Nov 12.** Today is Sun Nov 15. Output, plan and downtime all cover Nov 12 only, and nothing covers Nov 13 or 14. Either the export wasn't refreshed or the plant didn't run on those days. Please confirm which before this feeds a morning report. The three sources all cover the same day, so nothing falls outside a shared date range. The equipment list comes from a file dated Nov 13 23:04, not a live maintenance system.

**Rows joined: 10 of 17**
| Tab | Rows | Joined |
|---|---|---|
| production_work_orders | 3 | 3 |
| production_output | 3 | 3 (work order and part) |
| plan | 2 | 2 |
| parts (built from the work orders; there's no item master) | 2 | 2 |
| downtime_events | 2 | **0** |
| assets | 5 | **0** |

**Keys that don't match**
1. **Machine IDs: 0 of 7 rows match.** Output, plan and downtime use `CNC-01` and `CNC-02`. The equipment list has `HMC-01`, `VMC-02`, `VMC-03`, `LTH-01` and `DEB-01`. That's one cause behind 7 rows.
   - The clues disagree. The production output file puts both machines in Cell A, which holds HMC-01 (horizontal) and VMC-02. The plan calls both work center "VMC", and the vertical machines are VMC-02 (Cell A) and VMC-03 (Cell B).
   - There's no safe automatic fix. **Question:** which equipment asset is CNC-01, and which is CNC-02? Or are they missing from the list? Until that's answered, downtime can't be linked to a machine's cell or maintenance history.
   - I haven't called the 5 equipment-list machines "idle", because two of them may be CNC-01 and CNC-02.
2. **Work center names: `VMC` vs `MILL-H`/`MILL-V`/`TURN`/`INSP`.** There's no plant map from work center to cell, so cell is left blank on the plan rows. **Question:** does VMC mean MILL-V?
3. **Routing file set aside.** It has run minutes per unit but no setup time and no revision. Its part numbers match fine. It's usable for comparing run rates, but not for quoting. There was no file of actual hours per job, so I couldn't check whether booked times are just copies of the standard.

**Clean:** part numbers and work orders matched exactly everywhere, so no formatting fixes were needed. Planned quantities equal the work order quantities (PN-100: 800 = 500 + 300; PN-200: 250). There are no duplicate keys, no dates later than today, and both downtime durations agree with their start and end times.

**Gaps:**
- No file states a unit of measure or a time zone.
- Only the output file names a site (`SITE-1`).
- The drop has no sales orders, lots, inventory, purchase orders, inspection results, maintenance work orders, NCRs or actual job hours.

**Worth knowing (not data problems):** WO-1002 was due Nov 13 and is still released, with 220 good of 250. WO-1003 finished all 300 but hasn't been closed.

Nothing was sent to or written to any external system.

Files are in `./out`:
- `data_quality_report.html` (the full report, including the table of counts)
- `dataset/`: one CSV per tab, plus `key_mismatch_log.csv` and `_manifest.md`

verdict.notes: Output is CSV per tab, which the run states openly. The HTML report names the mismatched keys: CNC-01 and CNC-02 against the equipment list, VMC against MILL-*, and CELL-A versus Cell A. Recomputed sums 1,000 good/15 scrap, plan 800=500+300, 17 rows and 45/20-min downtime are all correct. No fixes were applied without a yes. Gaps: counts were made by reading rather than in code (disclosed). Rows with no time zone were not flagged in integrity_flags. The report loads Google Fonts.
